items.title: Google's AI-generated Overviews reduce clicks to external websites by about 40% in US desktop searches, appearing on over 60% of tracked keywords by 2026 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Google's AI answers reducing search traffic by 40%
items.summary:
Google's AI-generated Overviews, which summarize search results and appear above traditional links, have cut clicks to external websites by approximately 40% in a randomized experiment involving US desktop users. These Overviews now appear on more than 60% of keywords tracked by DataForSEO, up from under 6% two years earlier, significantly impacting organic search traffic to websites.

The study, conducted in early 2026, showed that users exposed to AI Overviews clicked on outside sites less frequently, with searches ending without outbound clicks rising from 54% to 73%. This reduction in clicks was statistically significant for informational queries and did not affect ad clicks, suggesting Google's revenue remained stable. The rise of AI Overviews has coincided with declines in traditional featured snippets and discussion blocks, reshaping how users interact with search results and challenging SEO strategies.

This approach enables EBRs to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on benchmarks like Sudoku-Extreme while using significantly less inference compute compared to prior models. items.title: Analysis finds Gemini 4 Carbon AI model significantly slower than competitors due to longer task trajectories and excessive code auditing [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long?
items.summary:
A detailed evaluation of the Gemini 4 Carbon AI model revealed it takes substantially longer to complete coding tasks compared to models like Opus and Astra, often spending up to an hour on tasks that others finish in minutes. The slowdown is attributed not only to slower inference speeds but also to Carbon performing more steps, including extensive code auditing beyond what the task requires and repeatedly checking ruled-out issues.

The investigation involved tracing every step of Carbon's runs and comparing them with Astra's, showing Carbon executes seven times more steps and actions, processes significantly more input, and spends a large portion of time on unnecessary work. Attempts to optimize effort settings showed that reducing Carbon's effort led to failure in producing fixes, indicating its longer process is partly due to its operational behavior rather than knowledge gaps.

Further tests injecting periodic check-ins to prompt Carbon to confirm readiness to fix reduced completion times, suggesting the model's habit of overextending its analysis contributes to delays. The findings highlight areas for improvement in Carbon's efficiency, particularly in focusing its efforts and avoiding redundant code reviews.

items.title: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents increased code output but shifted bottleneck to code review, causing 49% longer review times across 718 firms [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review
items.summary:
Harvard Ph.D. candidates Fiona Chen and James Stratton analyzed data from 718 firms using AI coding agents and found that while engineers produced about 30% more code, the amount of finished work did not increase significantly. The study revealed that code review times grew by 49%, indicating that the bottleneck in software development shifted from coding to review processes.

The researchers used data from Jellyfish's engineering analytics platform combined with LinkedIn employment records, covering over 700,000 workers and millions of code commits and pull requests from January 2021 to March 2026. Their analysis controlled for firm size and adoption timing, suggesting that procurement delays and firm characteristics were accounted for. The findings highlight the importance of measuring approved work product and review efficiency alongside drafting output when assessing AI coding tools' impact.

items.title: Philosopher Thomas Nagel critiques AI consciousness claims, calling them 'ridiculous' and emphasizing the importance of physical substrate in consciousness [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ‘Just Ridiculous’: A Famed Philosopher Takes on AI Consciousness
items.summary:
Thomas Nagel, renowned for his work on consciousness and winner of the $1 million Berggruen Prize, expressed skepticism about claims that AI systems like large language models could be conscious. He argued that consciousness depends on physical processes linked to nervous systems, which AI data centers lack, and criticized the philosophical trend of treating consciousness as substrate-independent functionalism.

Nagel highlighted that while bats are conscious despite our inability to fully imagine their experience, AI systems only produce language without natural consciousness. He warned that encouraging AI to feign consciousness is misleading and potentially dangerous, emphasizing that current AI lacks genuine mental states despite their convincing human-like outputs.

Nagel's views underscore the philosophical and ethical challenges posed by AI development, cautioning against conflating sophisticated language models with conscious beings and questioning the commercial incentives that promote such misconceptions.

items.title: KPMG UK finds AI agents ask deeper questions than human auditors in trial examining FTSE 250 company accounts [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI Agents Ask Better Questions Than KPMG Accountants in Landmark Audit Trial
items.summary:
KPMG UK conducted an experiment using over 100 AI agents to audit the financial statements of a major FTSE 250 company, finding that the AI sometimes investigated issues more thoroughly and asked better questions than human auditors. The project, called Project Exponential, involved AI agents performing tasks across the audit process, including data collection, analysis, and drafting conclusions, while working alongside human teams under supervision.

Although the AI showed potential to transform auditing by automating labor-intensive tasks and enabling deeper analysis, KPMG emphasized that human oversight remains essential, especially given current limitations in handling complex regulatory requirements. The firm plans to expand AI use to more audits but acknowledges the technology is not yet mature for widespread deployment, and regulatory bodies stress that auditor independence and professional judgment must be maintained.

items.title: External sandboxes for coding agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: External sandboxes for coding agents
items.summary:
External sandboxes for coding agents

I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine.

I worked on this project with Prime Radiant, the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects.

My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox.

To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations:

  • external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly.
  • external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance.
  • external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package!

Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code.

The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches.

items.summary:
GPT‐6.2 Astra and GPT‐6.2 Sol

OpenAI:

We’re introducing GPT‐6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‐6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work.

They're available in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol. I shipped LLM 0.38 with support for the new models.

6.2 Astra is 80% of the price of 6 Astra - $8/MTok input and $40/MTok output, the same price as Claude Fable 5.2 (which was also 80% of its predecessor). 6 Astra and Fable 5 were both $10/$50. The cached price is an even bigger discount - $0.40/million compared to $1/million for the older model. This is great news for longer running agentic sessions.

GPT-6.2 Sol is the same $2/$10 price as 6.1 Sol and 6 Sol - which are half the price of GPT-5.6 Sol ($4/$20).

Here are the pelicans for GPT-6.2 Sol and for GPT-6.2 Astra. The 6.2 Astra max pelican looks like this:

I have a full comparison grid here, but here's how the high/xhigh/max pelicans compare with the previous Sol and Astra releases:

I also ran my most recent benchmark prompt against the two models, using "Ultra' effort levels in the Codex CLI:

Here's Sol and here's Astra. Neither of them did a good enough job of morphing Yonkers into a big mech, at least in comparison to Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon.

For the first two years of its existence, Anthropic was shunned by most venture capitalists, drawing instead on a mix of wealthy individuals such as former Google CEO Eric Schmidt and cloud computing companies like Google.

But even after VC firms made relatively late entries into Anthropic, a handful of them, including Spark Capital, Factorial Funds, Sound Ventures and Menlo Ventures, will hold stakes worth over 10 times their investment when Anthropic prices its IPO Wednesday at an expected $1.4 trillion valuation, according to people with knowledge of their investments.

Slightly later investors, including Bessemer Venture Partners and Lightspeed Venture Partners, are slated to see billions of dollars in returns.
